**How many queries of each kind ran** — a count, not time. For where the time went, see 'Query Time by Type' on the Overview.

**Normal:** query_columns = tables scanned + tables failed; list_tables = owner attempts; the metadata kinds = owners with tables, when the scan has DBA access.

targets.expr: sum by (query_type) (sum_over_time(((last_over_time(oracle_scanner_query_duration_seconds_count{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$oracle_pod", query_type=~"$oracle_query_type"}[15s]) - last_over_time(oracle_scanner_query_duration_seconds_count{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$oracle_pod", query_type=~"$oracle_query_type"}[1d] offset 15s)) >= 0 or last_over_time(oracle_scanner_query_duration_seconds_count{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$oracle_pod", query_type=~"$oracle_query_type"}[15s]) * 1)[$__range:15s])) > 0

panels.description:
**How long samples took, split into successes and failures**, so fast failures do not make successes look quicker than they are.

**Normal:** only readable under sustained load.

panels.title: Stream Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description:
**Only the part spent reading rows from Oracle and uploading them.** The whole fetch minus this is setup: credentials, connection, looking up the column type.

**Normal:** most of the fetch time on big tables; little on small ones.

panels.title: Stream Throughput
panels.description:
**Speed while streaming, adjusted for size.**

**Normal:** steady. If fetches get slower and this holds, the samples just got bigger; if this drops, something really got slower.

panels.description:
**Size of each successful sample, over time.** **How to read it:** each box is 'this many samples were this big, at this moment'; brighter = more, hover for the exact count.

**Normal:** values are cut at 4000 characters, so a text/CLOB sample tops out around rows × 4000 bytes.

### Oracle Connector — Runtime
Generated from `dashboards/applications/V2/connectors/oracle/oracle-runtime.json` · per-cluster board: [Oracle Connector — Runtime](/d/apps-v2-oracle-runtime)

**Is the connector itself healthy?** CPU, memory, Go runtime and file handles for the scanner and content pods. Use the *component* selector at the top to look at one of them.

**Empty is normal:** both deployments scale to zero between jobs, so this board only has data while something runs.

Hover the ⓘ on any panel for what it shows, what is normal, and where to look next.

panels.title: Process CPU (rate)
panels.description:
**CPU the connector process uses**, in cores.

**Normal:** near 0 when idle, up to the limit (0.5 core for scanner and content) during work. Pinned at the limit means the pod is being throttled and everything slows down.

**Next:** 'Container CPU Usage' for what Kubernetes sees.

panels.title: Process Resident Memory
panels.description:
**Memory the process is really using** (what is in RAM).

**Normal:** well below the 1 GiB limit. A line that only goes up across several scans points at memory that is never released — e.g. the scans the pod keeps cached (see 'Job Contexts Active' on the Overview).

**Next:** 'Container Memory (working set)' — the number Kubernetes kills on.

panels.title: Process Virtual Memory
panels.description:
**Memory the process has reserved**, used or not. Go reserves far more than it uses.

**Normal:** large and flat. Not a useful alarm on its own — use resident memory.

panels.title: Container CPU Usage
panels.description:
**CPU per pod as Kubernetes measures it.** These container panels select pods by name, because Kubernetes' own metrics do not carry the connector's labels.

**Normal:** same shape as Process CPU. At 0.5 core the pod is at its limit.

panels.title: Container Memory (working set)
panels.description:
**Memory per pod as Kubernetes measures it** — the number it compares with the 1 GiB limit.

**Normal:** well below 1 GiB. Reaching it gets the pod killed (OOMKilled) and the work it held is retried.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description:
**How many concurrent tasks the program is running.**

**Normal:** grows during a scan and returns to a low, steady number after. A count that keeps growing between scans is a leak.

panels.title: Heap In-Use
panels.description:
**Memory used by the program's own data.**

**Normal:** rises during work and drops after garbage collection. Steadily rising floors across scans mean something is being kept.

panels.title: GC Pause — max & median
panels.description:
**How long the program stops to clean up memory.** Max = the worst pause, median = a typical one.

**Normal:** milliseconds. Pauses of hundreds of milliseconds mean memory pressure.

panels.title: Open vs Max FDs
panels.description:
**Open files and network connections against the process limit.**

**Normal:** far below the limit. Each Oracle connection is one of these, so it grows with 'Peak Connections /20' on the Overview.

panels.title: OS Threads
panels.description:
**Operating-system threads the program uses.**

**Normal:** a small, steady number. Growing steadily means calls are blocking.

panels.title: Probe Duration by Depth
panels.description: Time spent discovering objects (databases, schemas, tables, columns) after the connection is open, by requested depth. Credential fetch and the connect itself are excluded.

panels.title: Peak Tests In Flight
panels.description: Most connection tests this connector was answering at once in the selected range.

Content Stream Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Wall-clock duration of the streaming pipeline (Snowflake row pull + UploadFrom). The two legs run concurrently through an io.Pipe, so this reflects the slower of the two at any moment. Replaces the old separate Query Duration and Upload Duration metrics, which can't be measured independently in the streaming architecture.

panels.title: Content Stream Bytes — p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Bytes streamed per successful content fetch (Info.Size echoed back by the content transfer service). Useful for sizing impact of large-payload streaming and spotting outliers.

panels.title: Content Stream Rows — Rate (rows/s)
panels.description: Total rows streamed per second across successful content fetches.

panels.title: Content Stream Rows — Avg per Fetch
panels.description: Average rows streamed per successful content fetch (sum / count over a 5-minute window).

panels.title: Sample Verify-Empty by Outcome (count, 5m)
panels.description: Count of times the verify-at-100% branch fired during content sampling. outcome="recovered" means phase-1 SAMPLE SYSTEM returned zero rows on a non-empty table and the re-run rescued data — sustained > 0 means SamplePercent is too low for the row distribution. outcome="empty" means the re-run also returned nothing — table is genuinely empty, no action needed. Replaces the old sample_fallback_total metric.

panels.title: Registration State by Pod
panels.description:
**Whether each pod has registered itself with the registration service**, shown as the current state over time: registered, pending (no answer yet), unreachable (the registry or network is failing), rejected (the registry refused, retrying), rejected_final (refused for good), build_failed (the registration could not be built), lane_missing (no test-connection lane is being served), disabled (registration is switched off).

The registration series exist only on builds that include the registration-metrics change, so older pods show No data here. Connector pods scale to zero, so a pod's line exists only while a scanner pod is running.

**Normal:** registered, after a short pending at start-up. lane_missing, rejected_final and build_failed are the states to alert on: no other panel reports them, and the pod is not registering. unreachable held for longer than a deploy takes is worth alerting on too.

**Next:** 'Registration Attempts by Result' for whether attempts are still failing, and the connector logs for the reason.

targets.expr: (max by (pod) (snowflake_registration_state{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$snowflake_pod",state="disabled"}) * 1) + on(pod) (max by (pod) (snowflake_registration_state{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$snowflake_pod",state="pending"}) * 2) + on(pod) (max by (pod) (snowflake_registration_state{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$snowflake_pod",state="unreachable"}) * 3) + on(pod) (max by (pod) (snowflake_registration_state{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$snowflake_pod",state="rejected"}) * 4) + on(pod) (max by (pod) (snowflake_registration_state{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$snowflake_pod",state="registered"}) * 5) + on(pod) (max by (pod) (snowflake_registration_state{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$snowflake_pod",state="rejected_final"}) * 6) + on(pod) (max by (pod) (snowflake_registration_state{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$snowflake_pod",state="build_failed"}) * 7) + on(pod) (max by (pod) (snowflake_registration_state{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$snowflake_pod",state="lane_missing"}) * 8)

panels.title: Registration Attempts by Result
panels.description:
**Registration attempts made in the selected range**, by result: success (the registry accepted it), rejected (the registry refused it), failed (no answer: the registry was unreachable or failing). Totals add up every attempt of every pod in the range.

**Normal:** a success at start-up and one about every 6 hours when the pod renews. Rejected or failed attempts that keep coming mean the pod is not (re-)registering. A pod can still read registered while renewals fail, so this is the panel that shows it.

**Next:** 'Registration Attempts (rate, 5m)' beside it for when, and 'Registration State by Pod' for the pod's current state.

targets.expr: sum by (result) (sum_over_time(((last_over_time(snowflake_registration_attempts_total{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$snowflake_pod"}[15s]) - last_over_time(snowflake_registration_attempts_total{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$snowflake_pod"}[1d] offset 15s)) >= 0 or last_over_time(snowflake_registration_attempts_total{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$snowflake_pod"}[15s]) * 1)[$__range:15s])) > 0

panels.title: Registration Attempts (rate, 5m)
panels.description:
**When registration attempts happened**, by result, stacked. An attempt is rare, so a single one can read near 0 here and still be counted in 'Registration Attempts by Result'.

**Normal:** a short green mark at start-up and every 6 hours. A steady orange or red line means the pod keeps trying and the registry keeps refusing it or not answering.

**Next:** 'Registration State by Pod'; the registration service board for its side.

panels.title: Since Last Success
panels.description:
**How long since any pod last registered successfully**, measured from the newest success among the selected pods.

**Normal:** under 6 hours, because the connector re-registers every 6 hours. Well beyond that means renewals are failing even if the state still reads registered. No data means no scanner pod is running (they scale to zero) or the pod's build predates the registration metrics.

**Next:** 'Registration Attempts by Result' for what the attempts are returning.
